name: Gojiberry
what: Finds B2B buyers (people buying for their company) who are showing buying signals on LinkedIn, so sales teams know who to message.
title: Gojiberry's waitlist of 2,000 paid nothing. A rebuild took it to $407K in one month
dek: The first product got a big waitlist and zero sales. The team rebuilt it in weeks, then pushed it through Reddit and a dozen other channels at once. Its MRR (monthly recurring revenue: what subscribers pay every month) was $424,368 at the last Stripe sync. A month's revenue is the money actually collected that month, so the two numbers don't match exactly.
pattern: Throw away the first version when nobody pays

cost_to_start.label: Claimed

first_customers.text: The first version had a 2,000-person waitlist and made $0. After a rebuild around buying signals it reached 100+ paying customers in 60 days. The founder says Reddit helped bring the first 100.

phases.name: Done it before
phases.story: The founders' earlier company, Coco AI, sold WhatsApp marketing to online shops. It reached about €500,000 a year in revenue through cold outreach (messaging people who didn't know them yet) and was sold to an American fund. So they already knew how to find customers by messaging them directly.

number.v: €500K ARR (yearly recurring revenue) at the previous company
number.label: Claimed

phases.lesson: Skills carry over: what you learn selling one thing makes the next thing easier to sell.

phases.name: The waitlist that made $0
phases.story: Version one was an AI sales assistant that joined calls, took notes and filled in the CRM (the software sales teams use to track customers). The homepage asked people to join a waitlist, and it grew from 1,147 in April to over 2,000 in May. When it launched, none of them paid.

number.v: "Join 1147+ founders, sales professionals, and start ups already on the waitlist."
number.label: Wayback

phases.lesson: A signup is not a sale. Ask for money as early as you can.

phases.name: Rebuild in weeks
phases.story: The team threw out the note-taker and rebuilt the product from scratch around one job: find people on LinkedIn who are showing signs they want to buy, and hand over their contact details. By June the homepage said 'Trusted by 30+ B2B companies'. By July it said 100+.

number.v: 100+ paying customers within 60 days of the rebuild
number.label: Claimed

phases.lesson: When nobody pays, change the product, not just the marketing.

phases.name: Reddit first
phases.story: The co-founder posted stories on Reddit instead of ads: what $1,250 of LinkedIn influencer posts got him, and being turned down by Y Combinator (a famous program that invests in startups) after an interview. He warmed up each account for 1 to 2 weeks before posting and replied to every comment. He says Reddit brought 11 million views and 40,000+ visitors.

number.v: one post: about 2,000 visitors and 10 to 15 customers
number.label: Claimed

phases.lesson: Tell true stories with proof; a rejection can be your best post.

phases.name: Twelve channels at once
phases.story: Once Reddit worked, the team added everything: 5,000 cold emails a day, about 800 LinkedIn messages a week from five accounts using its own tool, daily posts, five YouTube videos a week, SEO (getting found on Google), newsletters, influencers and affiliates (people paid a cut for each customer they bring). Most customers were on a $99-a-month plan.
phases.lesson: Use your own product to sell your product; it is the best demo you have.

phases.name: Y Combinator and fast growth
phases.story: Gojiberry joined Y Combinator's Spring 2026 batch. Revenue roughly doubled every two to three months. The homepage count went from '500+ small sales teams' in March 2026 to '3,500+ growing B2B sales teams' in November.
phases.lesson: Getting turned down once is not the end; apply again with better numbers.

checklist: Put up a one-page site for your idea with a price on it, not just a waitlist, and see if anyone clicks Buy.
If your waitlist doesn't pay, call five people on it and ask what they would pay for instead.
Write one honest Reddit post about something that went wrong for you, in a subreddit that allows it, and reply to every comment.
Spend a week commenting helpfully in that community before you post about your own project.
Use your own product to find your first customers, so the way you sell is also your demo.
List three channels you haven't tried yet and test one this week for a small amount of time or money.
